title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Fragment 107, communicated by N. Fuss (source given as A. m. T. I p. 335–336).

**Setting.** Let P(x) = 1 + x^α + x^β + x^γ + … be a series of distinct powers, each with coefficient 1. Write S = P^λ = Σ [n] x^n.

**Theorem.** The coefficients satisfy

n[n] = Σ_{κ∈{α,β,γ,…}, κ≤n} (λκ − (n−κ)) [n−κ] = Σ ((λ+1)κ − n) [n−κ], with [0] = 1.

**Proof.** Take logarithmic derivatives: dS/S = λ dP/P, so P·xS' = λ S·xP'. Now compare the coefficients of x^n on both sides.
- Left side: n[n] + Σ_κ (n−κ)[n−κ].
- Right side: Σ_κ λκ[n−κ].

Rearranging gives the formula.

**Corollary.** For λ a positive integer, the exponents occurring in P^λ are exactly the sums of λ terms taken from {0, α, β, …}. So P^λ contains every power x^n if and only if every n is such a sum; a missing power has [n] = 0. No coefficient is negative.

**Purpose.** This is a computational tool for additive (Waring-type) problems. With P = 1 + x + x^4 + x^9 + … and λ = 4, it is Euler's generating-function approach to the four-squares theorem: the problem becomes showing that [n] > 0 for all n, using the recurrence. The recurrence has mixed-sign coefficients ((λ+1)κ − n), so it does not by itself deliver positivity. The fragment stops at stating the reduction.
errors: No mathematical error. The recurrence is correct, and equivalent to n[n] = Σ((λ+1)κ−n)[n−κ].

Gap: the corollary's statements (exponents are sums of λ terms; no negative coefficients) hold only for positive integer λ. The theorem itself holds for arbitrary real λ, where coefficients can be negative (e.g. λ = −1). Euler silently switches meaning.
The terms with n−κ = 0 must be included, with [0] = 1. This is implicit in 'non fiunt negativi'.

ideas.what: Recurrence for the coefficients of an arbitrary power P^λ of a power series, obtained from P·S' = λ S·P'
ideas.modern_name: Euler/J.C.P. Miller recurrence for powering power series (Knuth TAOCP vol. 2, §4.7)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Knuth attributes it to Euler); also known as Miller's formula (J.C.P. Miller, 20th c.)
ideas.where_published: Euler uses the same logarithmic-derivative coefficient comparison in published works (e.g. the pentagonal-number/divisor-sum papers, and partition papers such as E191). Exact first published locus of the general power formula: unsure.

ideas.what: Using the support and positivity of the coefficients of P^λ (e.g. a theta-type series to the 4th power) to decide whether every integer is a sum of λ terms from a set
ideas.modern_name: Generating-function approach to additive bases / Waring and four-squares problems (precursor of the Jacobi theta-function method)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (in correspondence with Goldbach on four squares); Jacobi 1829 completed the theta method
ideas.where_published: Euler–Goldbach correspondence (c. 1750) discusses (1+x+x^4+x^9+…)^4; exact published papers unsure

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, correct statement of a known recurrence (credited to Euler in the literature) together with the known generating-function reformulation of additive problems. It is unfinished as a proof strategy, but Euler's attempt via this route is documented. Nothing new for specialists.
transcription_corrections: None significant. In the final formula, the first stacked coefficient lacks an explicit '+' before λα, matching the image; the meaning is (λα − (n−α))[n−α].
